title: Exploitable?
blurb: Read the code and the attacker's input, then predict what actually happens. Knowing a rule is one thing — seeing the exploit land is another.

levels.title: L1 · The injectable query
levels.prompt: What does this attacker input do?

blocks.label: The query (name comes from the request)
blocks.code:
var sql = $"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = '{name}'";
db.Users.FromSqlRaw(sql).ToList();

levels.explain: The interpolation happens in C# BEFORE EF sees it, so FromSqlRaw runs: WHERE Name = '' OR '1'='1'. The injected OR makes the condition always true, dumping every user. FromSqlRaw + string interpolation is the classic trap.

failStates.title: The input breaks out of the string
failStates.explain: The attacker's quote closes the literal, and OR '1'='1' is always true — so the WHERE matches every row, not one.

failStates.title: It's valid SQL — that's the problem
failStates.explain: The injected fragment forms a perfectly valid WHERE clause. No error; it just returns everything.

levels.title: L2 · The parameterized version
levels.prompt: Same attack, but the query changed. What happens now?

options.label: Returns no users — the input is treated as a literal name

levels.explain: FromSqlInterpolated turns the interpolated value into a SQL PARAMETER, not query text. The database looks for a user literally named ' OR '1'='1 — which doesn't exist — so it returns nothing. Same-looking code, opposite safety: this is the fix for L1.

failStates.title: FromSqlInterpolated parameterizes
failStates.explain: Despite the $-string, FromSqlInterpolated (unlike FromSqlRaw) binds the value as a parameter, so it can't be executed as SQL. The attack fails.

failStates.title: No error — just a literal match
failStates.explain: The whole string is treated as a single value to compare against Name. It's valid; it simply matches nothing.

levels.title: L3 · Whose order is it?
levels.prompt: User A (id 1) is logged in. Order 42 belongs to User B. What happens?

options.label: Returns User B's order — broken access control

levels.explain: [Authorize] only checks that A is logged in — not that order 42 is A's. Find(42) returns it regardless of owner, so A reads B's order. That's Insecure Direct Object Reference, a form of Broken Access Control (A01). The fix is to filter by owner.

failStates.title: [Authorize] ≠ ownership check
failStates.explain: [Authorize] confirms authentication, not that the resource belongs to this user. It happily lets A fetch order 42.

failStates.title: The order exists — it's just not A's
failStates.explain: Find(42) finds it and returns it. Nothing scopes the lookup to the current user, so there's no 404 and no block.

levels.title: L4 · When the check throws
levels.prompt: The auth service throws (its database is down). What happens to the edit?

blocks.label: The handler

options.label: The edit proceeds — it fails OPEN

levels.explain: The empty catch swallows the exception, so control falls straight through to doc.Update — the permission check is silently skipped and the edit happens. That's 'failing open': Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (A10, new in 2025). Security checks must fail CLOSED — deny on error.

failStates.title: Nothing blocks it
failStates.explain: The Forbid() only runs if CanEdit returns false. When CanEdit THROWS, the catch eats the exception and execution continues to the update.

failStates.title: The catch prevents the 500
failStates.explain: The empty catch swallows the exception, so there's no crash — worse, the code proceeds as if the check passed.
